questions.questionText: Your company needs to process thousands of high-definition video frames overnight. The processing software is fault-tolerant, and if a frame's processing is interrupted, it can simply be retried from the queue without issues. To minimize costs, which Compute Engine configuration should you choose?
options: Standard virtual machines
Spot virtual machines
Committed Use Discount (CUD) instances
Bare Metal instances
correctAnswers: Spot virtual machines

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are highly discounted compute instances that utilize Google's excess capacity. Because they can be preempted (terminated) at any time by Google, they are the perfect cost-saving choice for fault-tolerant, resumable batch jobs like video rendering.

why other options are wrong.Standard virtual machines: Standard VMs offer guaranteed uptime but are significantly more expensive. Since the workload is fault-tolerant, paying on-demand prices is unnecessary.
why other options are wrong.Committed Use Discount (CUD) instances: CUDs require a 1- or 3-year commitment. For a workload that just runs overnight and can be interrupted, Spot VMs offer deeper discounts without a long-term commitment.
why other options are wrong.Bare Metal instances: Bare Metal is used for specialized legacy workloads (like Oracle databases) that cannot run in virtualized environments, which does not apply here.

questions.questionText: When Google Cloud needs to reclaim the resources used by your Spot VM, it sends a preemption notice. How much time does your application have to gracefully shut down before the VM is forcibly terminated?
options: 10 seconds
30 seconds
60 seconds
5 minutes
correctAnswers: 30 seconds

explanation.general explanation: When Google Cloud reclaims a Spot or Preemptible VM, it sends an ACPI G2 Soft Off signal to the instance. The instance then has exactly 30 seconds to execute a shutdown script, save state, or gracefully terminate before a hard power off is executed.

why other options are wrong.10 seconds: This is incorrect; Google provides 30 seconds of notice.
why other options are wrong.60 seconds: This is incorrect; the grace period is strictly 30 seconds.
why other options are wrong.5 minutes: This is incorrect; Spot VMs do not provide a 5-minute shutdown window.

questions.questionText: You are migrating an on-premises legacy relational database to Compute Engine. The database does not support clustering or automatic failover. Which compute volatility configuration MUST you choose for this virtual machine?
options: Spot virtual machines
Preemptible virtual machines
Standard virtual machines
Spot virtual machines with a shutdown script
correctAnswers: Standard virtual machines

explanation.general explanation: A legacy relational database that does not support failover is a stateful, non-fault-tolerant application. You must use Standard VMs, which provide guaranteed uptime and Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

why other options are wrong.Spot virtual machines: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which would cause immediate downtime and potential data corruption for a non-replicated database.
why other options are wrong.Preemptible virtual machines: Preemptible VMs act similarly to Spot VMs (and have a 24-hour limit) and are entirely unsuitable for a primary database.
why other options are wrong.Spot virtual machines with a shutdown sc: A 30-second shutdown script is not enough to make a monolithic, legacy database highly available across preemptions.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following workloads are excellent candidates for using Spot virtual machines to save costs? (Select two)
options: Stateless web server tiers behind a Load Balancer
Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) runners
In-memory Redis caching layers
Primary Microsoft SQL Server databases
Legacy monolithic ERP systems
correctAnswers: Stateless web server tiers behind a Load Balancer
Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) runners

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are ideal for stateless, fault-tolerant workloads. Stateless web tiers can easily have nodes added or removed by a Managed Instance Group and Load Balancer without affecting users. CI/CD runners process jobs that can usually be retried if interrupted.

why other options are wrong.In-memory Redis caching layers: When a Spot VM is preempted, the in-memory cache is wiped out, causing massive cache misses and database spikes.
why other options are wrong.Primary Microsoft SQL Server databases: A primary database requires high availability and cannot tolerate sudden preemptions.
why other options are wrong.Legacy monolithic ERP systems: These systems are typically stateful, take a long time to start, and cannot handle sudden hardware terminations.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Your application consists of a critical API frontend and a set of background worker pods that process image uploads. You want to run the API frontend on guaranteed compute capacity, but you want to run the background workers on discounted capacity. How should you configure this?
options: Create two separate GKE node pools: one with Standard VMs and one with Spot VMs, using node taints to direct the pods.
Create a single GKE node pool with Spot VMs and configure the API frontend pods to 'opt-out' of preemption.
Deploy the API frontend to Cloud Run and the background workers to a standard GKE cluster.
Use a single GKE node pool with Standard VMs and apply a Spot discount tag to the background worker pods.
correctAnswers: Create two separate GKE node pools: one with Standard VMs and one with Spot VMs, using node taints to direct the pods.

explanation.general explanation: GKE allows you to create multiple node pools with different machine types and configurations. By creating one node pool with Standard VMs (for the critical API) and another with Spot VMs (for the fault-tolerant workers), and using taints/tolerations or node affinity, you can safely mix workloads in the same cluster to optimize costs.

why other options are wrong.Create a single GKE node pool with Spot: You cannot 'opt-out' individual pods from preemption if the underlying VM node is a Spot VM.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the API frontend to Cloud Run and: While possible architecturally, this splits the deployment platforms unnecessarily when GKE natively supports mixed node pools.
why other options are wrong.Use a single GKE node pool with Standard: Discounts apply to the VM node level, not at the Kubernetes pod level via tags.

questions.questionText: Both Spot VMs and Preemptible VMs offer significant discounts but can be terminated by Compute Engine. What is the primary difference in the volatility configuration between a Spot VM and a legacy Preemptible VM?
options: Preemptible VMs are strictly terminated after a maximum of 24 hours, whereas Spot VMs do not have a maximum runtime limit.
Spot VMs give a 5-minute warning before termination, whereas Preemptible VMs give a 30-second warning.
Spot VMs can only be used in Managed Instance Groups, whereas Preemptible VMs can be standalone.
Preemptible VMs include a guaranteed SLA of 99%, whereas Spot VMs have no SLA.
correctAnswers: Preemptible VMs are strictly terminated after a maximum of 24 hours, whereas Spot VMs do not have a maximum runtime limit.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are the modern replacement for Preemptible VMs. While both can be preempted at any time due to capacity needs, a key improvement of Spot VMs is that they do not have the strict 24-hour maximum runtime limit that Preemptible VMs enforce.

why other options are wrong.Spot VMs give a 5-minute warning before: Both types provide a 30-second preemption notice.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs can only be used in Managed Ins: Both can be used as standalone VMs or inside Managed Instance Groups.
why other options are wrong.Preemptible VMs include a guaranteed SLA: Neither Spot nor Preemptible VMs have a Service Level Agreement (SLA).

questions.questionText: Your organization is highly focused on compliance and Service Level Agreements (SLAs). If you architect a solution entirely using Spot VMs across multiple regions, what SLA does Google Cloud guarantee for the Compute Engine instances?
options: No SLA is provided.
99.9% uptime SLA.
99.99% uptime SLA.
99.0% uptime SLA.
correctAnswers: No SLA is provided.

explanation.general explanation: Because Spot VMs run on excess compute capacity and can be reclaimed by Google at any time, they are explicitly excluded from the Compute Engine Service Level Agreement (SLA). There is no financial or uptime guarantee.

This applies to single Standard VMs, not Spot VMs.
This applies to Standard VMs deployed across multiple zones, not Spot VMs.
This is an arbitrary number; Spot VMs have zero SLA.

questions.questionText: To effectively use Spot VMs in your architecture without impacting user experience, your application design MUST exhibit which TWO of the following characteristics? (Select two)
options: Stateless processing
Idempotency
Strict dependency on Local SSD data
Long-running synchronous user sessions
Manual administrative recovery procedures
correctAnswers: Stateless processing
Idempotency

explanation.general explanation: To survive the volatile nature of Spot VMs, applications should be stateless (so any node can pick up the work) and idempotent (so if a job is interrupted and retried, it does not cause data duplication or errors).

why other options are wrong.Strict dependency on Local SSD data: Local SSD data is lost when a Spot VM is preempted, making it fatal for the application.
why other options are wrong.Long-running synchronous user sessions: If a VM serving a long-running synchronous session is preempted, the user is disconnected and experiences an error.
why other options are wrong.Manual administrative recovery procedure: Spot architecture must rely on automated recovery (like Managed Instance Groups), not manual administrative intervention, which is too slow.

questions.questionText: You have configured a Managed Instance Group (MIG) with a target size of 10 Spot VMs. Suddenly, Google Cloud experiences a high demand for standard capacity in that zone and reclaims 4 of your Spot VMs. What action does the Managed Instance Group take?
options: The MIG will automatically attempt to recreate the 4 preempted Spot VMs in the background as soon as capacity becomes available.
The MIG will automatically replace the 4 Spot VMs with Standard VMs to maintain the target size of 10.
The MIG target size will be permanently reduced to 6 to reflect the lost capacity.
The MIG will delete the remaining 6 Spot VMs to prevent application inconsistencies.
correctAnswers: The MIG will automatically attempt to recreate the 4 preempted Spot VMs in the background as soon as capacity becomes available.

explanation.general explanation: When Spot VMs are part of a Managed Instance Group (MIG), the MIG continuously monitors the instances. If Spot VMs are preempted, the MIG does not give up; it will automatically and continuously attempt to launch new Spot VMs to restore the group to its target size of 10.

why other options are wrong.The MIG will automatically replace the 4: A MIG uses the exact Instance Template provided. It will not switch the provisioning model from Spot to Standard automatically to fill the gap.
why other options are wrong.The MIG target size will be permanently: The target size remains 10. The MIG will keep trying to reach 10.
why other options are wrong.The MIG will delete the remaining 6 Spot: The remaining VMs will continue to run and serve traffic; the MIG will simply try to replace the missing ones.

questions.questionText: You are running a 4-hour machine learning training job on a single Spot VM. Because the VM might be preempted at any moment, what best practice should you implement in your application code to minimize wasted compute time?
options: Implement checkpointing to frequently save the training state to Cloud Storage.
Write a shutdown script to delay the preemption by an additional 10 minutes.
Use a Local SSD to permanently store the training outputs.
Change the VM's volatility configuration to Standard mid-training if a preemption notice is received.
correctAnswers: Implement checkpointing to frequently save the training state to Cloud Storage.

explanation.general explanation: Checkpointing is a crucial best practice for long-running jobs on Spot VMs. By frequently saving the application state (checkpoints) to a durable storage service like Cloud Storage, a preempted job can simply resume from the last checkpoint rather than starting over from the beginning.

why other options are wrong.Write a shutdown script to delay the pre: You cannot delay a preemption. The shutdown script has a strict 30-second limit before hard termination.
why other options are wrong.Use a Local SSD to permanently store the: Local SSD data is ephemeral and is completely lost when a Spot VM is preempted.
why other options are wrong.Change the VM's volatility configuration: You cannot change a VM from Spot to Standard while it is running.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a managed Hadoop/Spark cluster using Dataproc to process massive amounts of batch data. To aggressively optimize costs, how should you apply Spot/Preemptible VMs within the Dataproc cluster architecture?
options: Configure the secondary worker nodes as Spot/Preemptible VMs.
Configure the primary (master) node as a Spot VM.
Configure all primary and standard worker nodes as Spot VMs.
Dataproc does not support Spot or Preemptible VMs.
correctAnswers: Configure the secondary worker nodes as Spot/Preemptible VMs.

explanation.general explanation: In a Dataproc cluster, secondary worker nodes are specifically designed to be non-data-storing, purely computational nodes. Using Spot or Preemptible VMs for secondary workers is the standard way to massively reduce Dataproc job costs without losing the critical cluster management components.

why other options are wrong.Configure the primary (master) node as a: If the primary node is preempted, the entire cluster fails.
why other options are wrong.Configure all primary and standard worke: Standard worker nodes store HDFS data. If they are preempted, data blocks can be lost. Only secondary workers should be Spot/Preemptible.
why other options are wrong.Dataproc does not support Spot or Preemp: This is false; Dataproc has native, deep integration for preemptible/spot secondary workers.

questions.questionText: When using a GKE node pool configured with Spot VMs, Google Cloud intercepts the 30-second preemption notice from Compute Engine. How much time does GKE typically give your pods to gracefully terminate before the underlying node shuts down?
options: 25 seconds
30 seconds
60 seconds
5 minutes
correctAnswers: 25 seconds

explanation.general explanation: When a Spot VM in a GKE cluster receives a preemption notice, the GKE kubelet is notified. GKE reserves about 5 seconds to gracefully handle node teardown, giving the running pods approximately 25 seconds of graceful termination time (SIGTERM) before the VM is shut off.

why other options are wrong.30 seconds: While the VM gets 30 seconds, the pods get slightly less (~25s) so the kubelet can finalize the shutdown.
why other options are wrong.60 seconds: The absolute maximum for the VM itself is 30 seconds, so pods cannot get 60 seconds.
why other options are wrong.5 minutes: Spot VMs do not provide a 5-minute preemption window.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following resources associated with a Spot VM will NOT survive if the VM is preempted? (Select two)
options: Data stored on a Local SSD attached to the VM
The ephemeral internal IP address assigned to the VM
Data stored on an attached Standard Persistent Disk
Data exported to a Cloud Storage bucket
Custom metadata applied to the VM configuration
correctAnswers: Data stored on a Local SSD attached to the VM
The ephemeral internal IP address assigned to the VM

explanation.general explanation: When a Spot VM is preempted and transitioning to the TERMINATED state, the ephemeral internal IP address is released. Additionally, any data stored on physically attached Local SSDs is permanently lost.

why other options are wrong.Data stored on an attached Standard Pers: Standard Persistent Disks are durable network storage. When the VM is preempted, the disk is detached, but the data remains completely intact.
why other options are wrong.Data exported to a Cloud Storage bucket: Cloud Storage is an external, durable object store and is unaffected by VM preemptions.
why other options are wrong.Custom metadata applied to the VM config: VM metadata is stored in the control plane and remains part of the instance configuration even when it is in a TERMINATED state.

questions.questionText: Mountkirk Games (Case Study) runs a global multiplayer backend. During peak hours, thousands of players are matched in real-time game sessions hosted on Compute Engine VMs. The sessions last roughly 45 minutes and dropping a player mid-game ruins the experience. Should they use Spot VMs for the game servers?
options: No, because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which would disconnect active players and ruin the experience.
Yes, because Spot VMs provide a 5-minute warning, which is enough time to migrate players to another server.
Yes, because Spot VMs guarantee at least 24 hours of uptime before preemption.
No, because Spot VMs cannot be placed behind a Global Load Balancer.
correctAnswers: No, because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which would disconnect active players and ruin the experience.

explanation.general explanation: Real-time, stateful game sessions where a disconnect ruins the user experience are NOT fault-tolerant workloads. Because Spot VMs can be preempted at any moment (with only 30 seconds notice), they are entirely unsuitable for hosting active Mountkirk Games multiplayer sessions.

why other options are wrong.Yes, because Spot VMs provide a 5-minute: Spot VMs provide exactly 30 seconds of warning, not 5 minutes.
why other options are wrong.Yes, because Spot VMs guarantee at least: Neither Spot nor Preemptible VMs guarantee *any* uptime. They can be preempted 1 minute after starting.
why other options are wrong.No, because Spot VMs cannot be placed be: Spot VMs absolutely can be placed behind load balancers, but the workload type (stateful gaming) makes them inappropriate.

questions.questionText: A Spot VM running a batch processing job suddenly shut down. The developer wants to know if the shut down was caused by an application crash, a manual user action, or a Google Cloud preemption event. Where should they look to confirm if a preemption occurred?
options: Check Cloud Logging for a `compute.instances.preempted` system event.
Check the VM's local syslog for a 'GCP_PREEMPTION' string.
Check Cloud Billing for a 'Preemption Refund' credit.
Check the Cloud Storage bucket for an automatically generated preemption dump file.
correctAnswers: Check Cloud Logging for a `compute.instances.preempted` system event.

explanation.general explanation: When Compute Engine preempts a Spot or Preemptible VM, it writes a specific system event (`compute.instances.preempted`) to Cloud Logging. Querying this log is the standard way to definitively verify that Google reclaimed the instance rather than it crashing for other reasons.

why other options are wrong.Check the VM's local syslog for a 'GCP_P: The ACPI signal might trigger normal OS shutdown logs, but the explicit preemption event is recorded in the GCP-level Cloud Logging system.
why other options are wrong.Check Cloud Billing for a 'Preemption Re: You are simply not billed after the VM stops; there is no explicit 'refund' line item that helps diagnose a crash in real-time.
why other options are wrong.Check the Cloud Storage bucket for an au: Google Cloud does not automatically generate or export memory dumps to Cloud Storage upon preemption.

questions.questionText: Your engineering team runs hundreds of automated integration tests every time code is committed. The tests take about 5 minutes to run and can be safely re-run if they fail. Which compute volatility configuration provides the most cost-effective way to run these ephemeral CI/CD pipelines?
options: Spot virtual machines
Standard virtual machines with Sole-Tenant Nodes
Committed Use Discount (CUD) instances
Shielded VMs
correctAnswers: Spot virtual machines

explanation.general explanation: CI/CD pipelines are ephemeral, short-lived, and fault-tolerant by nature (they can simply be re-triggered). Spot VMs are perfectly suited for this use case, providing massive cost discounts for running thousands of automated tests.

why other options are wrong.Standard virtual machines with Sole-Tena: Sole-Tenant nodes are for strict compliance/licensing isolation and are very expensive.
why other options are wrong.Committed Use Discount (CUD) instances: CUDs require a 1 or 3 year commitment for steady-state workloads, whereas CI/CD loads are often bursty and ephemeral.
why other options are wrong.Shielded VMs: Shielded VMs protect against rootkits and boot-level malware, which is a security feature, not a volatility/cost-optimization configuration.

questions.questionText: You have configured a shutdown script on a Spot VM to upload logs to Cloud Storage before the VM is preempted. The log upload process typically takes 45 seconds. What will happen when a preemption event occurs?
options: The script will fail to finish, because the VM will be forcibly terminated after exactly 30 seconds.
The script will complete successfully, because Google Cloud waits for the shutdown script to exit before terminating the VM.
The script will be paused, the VM will be suspended, and the script will resume when capacity is restored.
The script will complete successfully, because Spot VMs provide a 60-second grace period.
correctAnswers: The script will fail to finish, because the VM will be forcibly terminated after exactly 30 seconds.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs provide a strict 30-second notice before preemption. If a shutdown script takes longer than 30 seconds (like the 45-second script in the scenario), it will be interrupted mid-execution, and the VM will be forcibly hard-powered off.

why other options are wrong.The script will complete successfully, b: Google Cloud does not wait for user scripts to finish. The 30-second limit is a hard cutoff.
why other options are wrong.The script will be paused, the VM will b: Spot VMs do not 'suspend' and resume later upon preemption; they enter the TERMINATED state.
why other options are wrong.The script will complete successfully, b: The grace period is 30 seconds, not 60 seconds.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following Google Cloud services allow you to natively provision and utilize Spot or Preemptible VMs under the hood to lower your overall workload costs? (Select two)
options: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Node Pools
Cloud Dataproc Secondary Workers
Cloud SQL Primary Instances
Cloud Spanner Processing Nodes
Cloud Storage Buckets
correctAnswers: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Node Pools
Cloud Dataproc Secondary Workers

explanation.general explanation: Both GKE and Cloud Dataproc have native, built-in features to consume Spot/Preemptible VMs. GKE allows you to create specialized Spot node pools for fault-tolerant pods, and Dataproc allows you to use them as secondary worker nodes to speed up batch processing cheaply.

why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL Primary Instances: Cloud SQL is a managed database service that requires high availability; it does not support Spot VMs.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Spanner Processing Nodes: Cloud Spanner provides highly available, global relational databases and does not run on interruptible Spot capacity.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage Buckets: Cloud Storage is an object storage service, not a compute service. It has storage classes (like Nearline), but not 'Spot' provisioning.

questions.questionText: Helicopter Racing League (Case Study) needs to run millions of predictive machine learning simulations overnight to calculate probabilities for the next race. The system distributes the independent simulations via a Pub/Sub queue. Which compute configuration is most appropriate for the worker nodes?
options: Spot virtual machines
Standard virtual machines
App Engine Standard environment
Cloud SQL
correctAnswers: Spot virtual machines

explanation.general explanation: Because the simulations are independent and distributed via a Pub/Sub queue, the architecture is fully decoupled and fault-tolerant. If a worker node fails, the message simply returns to the queue. Therefore, Spot VMs are the ideal choice to process this massive compute job at the lowest possible cost.

why other options are wrong.Standard virtual machines: Standard VMs would work perfectly but would be far more expensive and unnecessary given the fault-tolerant nature of the queued workload.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard environment: App Engine is optimized for serving HTTP web traffic, not for long-running, heavy machine learning simulations.
why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL: Cloud SQL is a relational database, not a compute platform for running custom ML simulations.

questions.questionText: You configure an auto-scaling Managed Instance Group using Spot VMs. During a major product launch event globally, your MIG attempts to scale out, but you notice error messages stating `ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED`. What is the cause of this error?
options: Google Cloud does not have enough spare Spot compute capacity in that specific zone at this moment.
You have exceeded your project's monthly billing budget limit.
Spot VMs cannot be used in a Managed Instance Group with auto-scaling enabled.
The MIG is trying to run a Spot VM for more than 24 hours.
correctAnswers: Google Cloud does not have enough spare Spot compute capacity in that specific zone at this moment.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are provisioned from Google Cloud's unused, excess capacity. If standard paying customers need that capacity, or if overall demand is high, the excess capacity pool runs dry. `ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED` means Google cannot fulfill your Spot VM request right now.

why other options are wrong.You have exceeded your project's monthly: Billing budget limits trigger alerts, but they do not automatically block infrastructure provisioning unless you have set up a custom programmatic kill-switch.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs cannot be used in a Managed Ins: This is false; Spot VMs are fully supported and commonly used in auto-scaling MIGs.
why other options are wrong.The MIG is trying to run a Spot VM for m: Spot VMs do not have a 24-hour limit (only legacy Preemptible VMs do), and even if they did, the error for that would not be an exhausted pool.

questions.questionText: You need to run a fault-tolerant workload that requires a highly specific CPU-to-memory ratio not found in Google Cloud's predefined machine types (e.g., e2-standard-4). You also want to utilize deep Spot pricing discounts. Can you combine Custom Machine Types with the Spot provisioning model?
options: Yes, you can configure a Custom Machine Type as a Spot VM to get discounts on the custom resources.
No, Spot VMs are strictly limited to the `e2-micro` and `f1-micro` predefined machine types.
No, Custom Machine Types can only be deployed as Standard VMs with on-demand pricing.
Yes, but you will only receive the Spot discount on the CPU, while memory will be billed at standard rates.
correctAnswers: Yes, you can configure a Custom Machine Type as a Spot VM to get discounts on the custom resources.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud provides great flexibility by allowing you to combine features. You can define a Custom Machine Type (specifying exact vCPUs and RAM) and simultaneously set its provisioning model to 'Spot', receiving the massive Spot discount on both the custom CPU and memory resources.

why other options are wrong.No, Spot VMs are strictly limited to the: Spot pricing applies to almost all machine families (N1, N2, E2, C2, etc.), not just micro instances.
why other options are wrong.No, Custom Machine Types can only be dep: Custom Machine Types are fully compatible with the Spot provisioning model.
why other options are wrong.Yes, but you will only receive the Spot: The Spot discount applies to the entire instance's compute resources (both vCPU and memory).

questions.questionText: Your team is running distributed AI model training. The training scripts require NVIDIA GPUs and are designed to automatically resume from checkpoints if interrupted. To reduce the massive cost of GPU training, can you attach GPUs to Spot VMs?
options: Yes, GPUs can be attached to Spot VMs, and both the VM and the GPU are billed at the discounted Spot rate.
No, GPUs are premium hardware and can only be attached to Standard, non-preemptible VMs.
Yes, but only the underlying VM receives the Spot discount; the GPU is always billed at the standard on-demand rate.
Yes, GPUs can be attached, but they disable the preemption feature, turning the VM into a Standard VM.
correctAnswers: Yes, GPUs can be attached to Spot VMs, and both the VM and the GPU are billed at the discounted Spot rate.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud allows you to attach GPUs to Spot (and Preemptible) VMs. When you do this, both the underlying compute instance (CPU/RAM) AND the attached GPU are billed at the heavily discounted Spot rate, making fault-tolerant ML training highly cost-effective.

why other options are wrong.No, GPUs are premium hardware and can on: Google explicitly supports attaching GPUs to preemptible/spot instances.
why other options are wrong.Yes, but only the underlying VM receives: The discount applies to the attached GPU pricing as well.
why other options are wrong.Yes, GPUs can be attached, but they disa: The VM and the GPU remain preemptible; Google can reclaim the GPU capacity at any time.

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following workloads would be highly UNSUITABLE for a Compute Engine Spot VM configuration? (Select two)
options: A core e-commerce transactional database.
An in-memory Memcached cluster storing user shopping carts.
A stateless image thumbnail generation service.
An Apache Spark batch job managed by Dataproc.
A CI/CD Jenkins agent compiling source code.
correctAnswers: A core e-commerce transactional database.
An in-memory Memcached cluster storing user shopping carts.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs can be suddenly terminated with only 30 seconds of warning. Therefore, they are highly unsuitable for stateful applications like transactional databases (where sudden termination causes data corruption/loss) and in-memory caches (where termination instantly wipes out the cache data).

why other options are wrong.A stateless image thumbnail generation s: Stateless microservices are the perfect use case for Spot VMs.
why other options are wrong.An Apache Spark batch job managed by Dat: Batch jobs are fault-tolerant and retryable, making them an excellent use case for Spot VMs.
why other options are wrong.A CI/CD Jenkins agent compiling source c: CI/CD agents are ephemeral and can simply restart failed jobs, making them great candidates for Spot VMs.

questions.questionText: You are designing a web application's frontend tier. You want to utilize Spot VMs to minimize costs, but you must ensure the application NEVER goes completely offline if Google Cloud experiences a massive capacity shortage and preempts all your Spot VMs. What is the simplest, most resilient architectural approach?
options: Deploy a baseline minimum number of Standard VMs alongside your Spot VMs behind the same Load Balancer.
Write a Cloud Function that converts the Spot VMs to Standard VMs when the capacity shortage occurs.
Use a single Managed Instance Group composed entirely of Spot VMs, but set the minimum size to 5.
Deploy the application exclusively on Preemptible VMs instead of Spot VMs.
correctAnswers: Deploy a baseline minimum number of Standard VMs alongside your Spot VMs behind the same Load Balancer.

explanation.general explanation: To balance cost savings with absolute reliability, the best practice is to run a baseline of Standard VMs (to guarantee the application never goes completely offline) and use Spot VMs to handle the bulk of the auto-scaling traffic. Both can serve traffic behind the same Load Balancer.

why other options are wrong.Write a Cloud Function that converts the: You cannot change the provisioning model of an existing VM on the fly. You would have to deploy new VMs, which takes time.
why other options are wrong.Use a single Managed Instance Group comp: Setting a minimum size to 5 does not prevent Google from preempting all of them if capacity is exhausted, taking the site offline.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the application exclusively on Pr: Preemptible VMs are also subject to preemption and do not guarantee uptime. They are legacy versions of Spot VMs.

questions.questionText: From a financial perspective, why would an architect choose to configure a workload on Spot virtual machines rather than Standard virtual machines without any committed use discounts?
options: Spot VMs generally provide an estimated 60% to 91% discount compared to standard on-demand pricing.
Spot VMs eliminate all egress network billing charges.
Spot VMs do not charge for any attached Persistent Disk storage.
Spot VMs are entirely free to use during weekend off-peak hours.
correctAnswers: Spot VMs generally provide an estimated 60% to 91% discount compared to standard on-demand pricing.

explanation.general explanation: The primary financial driver for using Spot VMs is the massive discount they offer. Because they run on Google's spare capacity and can be interrupted, they are priced dynamically, typically resulting in 60% to 91% savings compared to standard on-demand compute rates.

why other options are wrong.Spot VMs eliminate all egress network bi: Spot VMs are still subject to standard network egress pricing.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs do not charge for any attached: You still pay standard rates for any attached Persistent Disks, IP addresses, and other non-compute resources.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs are entirely free to use during: Spot VMs are never entirely free; they offer a steep discount but still incur charges based on usage.

questions.questionText: You are testing an application on a Spot VM. Before leaving for the day, you manually stop the instance from the Google Cloud Console. Does this manual stop trigger the 30-second preemption warning process?
options: No, a manual stop triggers a normal ACPI shutdown process, not a preemption event.
Yes, all Spot VMs are hard-terminated within 30 seconds regardless of how they are stopped.
No, but you will be charged a penalty fee for stopping a Spot VM manually.
Yes, stopping the VM manually logs a `compute.instances.preempted` event in Cloud Logging.
correctAnswers: No, a manual stop triggers a normal ACPI shutdown process, not a preemption event.

explanation.general explanation: Stopping a Spot VM manually via the console or API is treated as a normal instance stop, initiating a standard ACPI graceful shutdown. The 30-second preemption warning and explicit preemption event are only triggered when Google Cloud's infrastructure reclaims the instance.

why other options are wrong.Yes, all Spot VMs are hard-terminated wi: A user-initiated stop allows the OS to shut down normally according to standard Compute Engine rules, independent of the 30-second preemption limit.
why other options are wrong.No, but you will be charged a penalty fe: There are no penalty fees for stopping instances in Google Cloud.
why other options are wrong.Yes, stopping the VM manually logs a `co: A manual stop logs a normal user-initiated stop event, not a preemption event.

questions.questionText: After a Spot VM is successfully preempted by Google Cloud, what is the resulting state of the virtual machine instance?
options: TERMINATED
SUSPENDED
DELETED
MIGRATING
correctAnswers: TERMINATED

explanation.general explanation: When Google Cloud preempts a Spot or Preemptible VM, it stops the VM. The final state of the instance is `TERMINATED`. It still exists in your project (unless configured to auto-delete), and you stop paying for the vCPU and memory, though you continue paying for the attached persistent disk.

why other options are wrong.SUSPENDED: Suspend saves the memory state to disk. Spot VMs do not suspend upon preemption; they are completely shut down.
why other options are wrong.DELETED: The VM is not automatically deleted (unless you are using a Managed Instance Group or explicitly set auto-delete), it is just stopped.
why other options are wrong.MIGRATING: Spot VMs are not live-migrated to other hosts; they are preempted.

questions.questionText: Your team wrote a data processing script that takes exactly 2 hours to complete. They decide to run it on a Spot VM. However, the VM keeps getting preempted around the 1 hour and 50 minute mark, forcing the script to start over from the beginning every time. What is the most cost-effective solution?
options: Modify the script to periodically save its progress (checkpointing) to Cloud Storage so it can resume upon restart.
Upgrade the VM to a Standard VM with a Sole-Tenant node to avoid preemption.
Contact Google Cloud support to request a preemption exclusion for this specific VM.
Run the script on a Preemptible VM instead, which guarantees 24 hours of uptime.
correctAnswers: Modify the script to periodically save its progress (checkpointing) to Cloud Storage so it can resume upon restart.

explanation.general explanation: The core design principle for leveraging Spot VMs is fault tolerance. By modifying the script to checkpoint its progress periodically, the job can simply resume from the last saved state (e.g., at 1 hour 45 minutes) when the VM is recreated, preserving the massive Spot cost savings.

why other options are wrong.Upgrade the VM to a Standard VM with a S: This would guarantee completion but drastically increase costs, ignoring the cost-effective requirement.
why other options are wrong.Contact Google Cloud support to request: Google Cloud does not offer preemption exclusions or VIP statuses for individual Spot VMs.
why other options are wrong.Run the script on a Preemptible VM inste: Preemptible VMs do NOT guarantee 24 hours of uptime; they simply force-terminate *at* 24 hours if they haven't been preempted sooner.

questions.questionText: Google Cloud occasionally performs host maintenance events on the physical servers running your virtual machines. How does Compute Engine handle a Spot VM during a standard host maintenance event?
options: The Spot VM is preempted (terminated) instead of being live migrated.
The Spot VM is live migrated to another healthy physical host without downtime.
The Spot VM is paused for 5 minutes and then automatically resumed.
The Spot VM is temporarily converted into a Standard VM during the maintenance window.
correctAnswers: The Spot VM is preempted (terminated) instead of being live migrated.

explanation.general explanation: Standard VMs benefit from Live Migration, meaning they are seamlessly moved to another physical host during maintenance without downtime. Spot and Preemptible VMs do not receive this premium feature; instead, they are simply preempted (terminated) when a host maintenance event occurs.

why other options are wrong.The Spot VM is live migrated to another: Spot VMs are explicitly excluded from the Live Migration feature.
why other options are wrong.The Spot VM is temporarily converted int: Google does not automatically convert billing/provisioning models during maintenance.

questions.questionText: A colleague is confused about the difference between the newer Spot VMs and the older Preemptible VMs regarding their lifespan. Which statement correctly clarifies this configuration detail?
options: Preemptible VMs will always be terminated after 24 hours of running, whereas Spot VMs can potentially run for weeks if capacity allows.
Spot VMs will always be terminated after 24 hours of running, whereas Preemptible VMs can run indefinitely.
Both Spot and Preemptible VMs are strictly terminated after 24 hours.
Both Spot and Preemptible VMs guarantee at least 24 hours of uninterrupted runtime.
correctAnswers: Preemptible VMs will always be terminated after 24 hours of running, whereas Spot VMs can potentially run for weeks if capacity allows.

explanation.general explanation: The defining limitation of legacy Preemptible VMs is a hard cap of 24 hours; Google will forcefully terminate them at that mark regardless of capacity. Spot VMs remove this restriction, meaning they will only be terminated if Google needs the capacity, allowing them to potentially run for much longer uninterrupted.

why other options are wrong.Both Spot and Preemptible VMs are strict: Spot VMs do not have the 24-hour termination limit.
why other options are wrong.Both Spot and Preemptible VMs guarantee: Neither guarantees any uptime. They can both be preempted 10 seconds after starting.
